text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Safety note: an intermittent crank-no-start on a 2009 Honda Civic can leave the vehicle stalled in traffic or stranded in rain, and any under-hood water intrusion near the ignition coil, crank sensor, or under-hood fuse/relay box should be treated as urgent until verified.
- Most likely root cause is moisture intrusion affecting the crankshaft position sensor circuit or its connector/harness at the lower front of the R18 engine, with 46% confidence.
- The physical failure mechanism fits the rain-related pattern: water enters a cracked CKP sensor connector seal, chafed harness insulation, or corroded terminal cavity near the crank pulley, the 5 V/reference or signal waveform drops out during cranking, the PCM loses engine speed input, and injector pulse/ignition timing are withheld even though the starter motor cranks normally. Once the connector dries or makes contact again, the engine starts and then runs normally because the signal stabilizes.
- No OBD-II codes were provided, and that does not rule this in or out. A brief CKP dropout during a failed start may not mature a P0335/P0336 if the event clears before the PCM completes fault logic, especially on older Honda logic strategies.
- The “alternator test inconclusive” detail is lower-value evidence here because a charging-system fault usually causes slow crank, low-voltage warning behavior, or repeated dead-battery events, not a clean crank-no-start that is strongly rain-related.
- Age is a major factor on a 2009 Civic: rubber connector seals, loom tape, and lower-engine harness clips are now well past 15 years old, and Honda engine-bay connectors in splash zones commonly develop green copper oxide, increased resistance, and intermittent open circuits.
- More data is required because confidence is below 80%.
- Data Needed
- A scan-tool capture during a no-start showing live RPM while cranking; 0 rpm strongly supports CKP signal loss.
- A lab-scope pattern of the CKP signal during a wet-condition crank event, plus voltage-drop readings on sensor ground and reference circuits.
- Close photos of the CKP connector, lower front engine harness routing, splash shield condition, and any oil or water contamination near the crank pulley.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Secondary cause is ignition coil or coil-on-plug well moisture intrusion, 31% confidence. On the 2009 Civic 1.8L R18, a leaking cowl seal, hood seal, or aged coil boot can allow moisture into a plug tube, causing spark leakage to ground during cranking. This fits “runs fine once started” because heat can dry the boot and raise insulation resistance. It ranks below CKP because many coil-related no-starts also produce a rough run or misfire DTC such as P0301-P0304/P0300, and none were reported.
- Tertiary cause is under-hood fuse/relay box or PGM-FI main relay power-feed intermittency from moisture/corrosion, 23% confidence. The mechanism is water intrusion at the under-hood fuse box, relay cavity, or PCM power feed causing intermittent loss of fuel pump or ECM/PCM power during crank. This is a known rain-sensitive failure mode on older Hondas, but it ranks below the top two because the symptom description emphasizes random rain-related no-start without mention of dash resets, fuel-pump prime loss, or accessory power anomalies.
- A less likely fourth-tier idea, not in the top three, is charging-voltage instability from alternator/regulator issues. A failing regulator can create low system voltage during crank, but that usually leaves low-voltage evidence below 9.6 V, dim lamps, or repeated battery discharge, which is not the strongest fit after a new battery and starter.
- Equipment-specific pattern: 2006-2011 Civic models commonly show age-related ignition coil boot tracking, lower-engine sensor harness deterioration, and relay/fuse-box corrosion rather than true mechanical engine faults when the complaint is intermittent and weather-sensitive.
- The absence of warning lamps slightly favors an intermittent input/power fault over a hard component failure because many hard failures set a MIL after one or two drive cycles.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Test 1: During a no-start, connect an enhanced scan tool and monitor engine RPM, CKP sync, injector pulse command, and immobilizer status while cranking. Expected reading for a healthy CKP circuit is roughly 150-250 rpm during crank. If RPM stays at 0 rpm with normal cranking speed, the primary CKP diagnosis moves to the top. If RPM is present and stable, look harder at coils or power-feed faults. Typical diagnostic charge: $80-$140.
- Test 2: Backprobe the CKP sensor circuit and capture the waveform with a 2-channel lab scope during dry and wet simulation. Depending on engine variant, the shop should verify a clean digital or AC-style pulse pattern without dropout, plus stable sensor ground below 0.1 V drop. If misting the connector/harness with water causes signal collapse, that confirms moisture intrusion. Scope testing usually adds $90-$180.
- Test 3: Perform ignition output testing with an adjustable spark tester set around 25-30 kV and inspect all four coil boots for carbon tracking, water trails, and oil contamination in the plug wells. Strong spark on all four during a no-start points away from coil moisture; weak or absent spark on one or more cylinders with wet boots supports the secondary cause. Cost: $60-$120.
- Test 4: Verify PGM-FI/PCM/fuel-pump power feeds with a multimeter and voltage-drop test at the under-hood fuse/relay box during crank. Battery voltage should remain above about 9.6 V, and power-feed drop across suspect terminals should stay under 0.2 V. A sudden loss of relay output or excessive drop during wet testing supports the tertiary cause. Cost: $70-$140.
- Test 5: Use a smoke-free water intrusion simulation around the cowl, fuse box, coil cover area, and lower splash zone while the scope and scan tool are connected. This is the key separating test because it reproduces the rain condition without guessing. Cost: $40-$90 when combined with the above.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- Ask: “Can you show me the live RPM value during the failed crank event, and was it 0 rpm or around 150-250 rpm?” They should provide a scan-tool screenshot or printout. Red flag: “It cranked, so the crank sensor is fine.”
- Ask: “Did you scope the CKP signal at the sensor or PCM, and do you have the waveform before and during water simulation?” They should show an actual waveform capture with time scale and voltage scale. Red flag: “We don’t need a scope for that.”
- Ask: “What was battery voltage during crank, and what was the voltage drop on the PCM or relay power feed?” They should give numbers such as 10.4 V cranking and under 0.2 V drop. Red flag: “Voltage looked okay” with no readings.
- Ask: “Did you test spark with an adjustable tester and inspect the coil boots and plug wells for tracking or moisture?” They should show photos of the boots/plugs. Red flag: replacing coils without boot inspection.
- Ask: “How did you reproduce the rain condition—water simulation at the cowl, fuse box, or lower harness?” They should describe the exact area wetted and the result. Red flag: “We couldn’t duplicate it, so we recommend an alternator.”

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: “I’ve done some research and want to understand whether the no-start is losing crankshaft RPM signal, ignition output, or PGM-FI power during wet conditions.”
- Phrasing: “I’m not trying to second-guess the diagnosis; I’m curious which test separated the CKP circuit from the coil boots and the fuse-box relay feeds.”
- Example dialogue: “Can you show me the scan data during crank, specifically RPM and immobilizer status?” “Did the RPM stay at 0, or did it read around 200 rpm?” “Do you have a scope capture of the CKP waveform before and after water simulation?” “Were the coil boots dry, and did you see any carbon tracking in the plug wells?” “What voltage did the PCM or relay output hold during crank?”
- Body language: keep your phone down, hold a notepad, and ask for readings in volts, rpm, and waveform screenshots. That signals you expect measured data, not parts guessing.
- Response handling: if they get defensive, say, “I’m only trying to approve the right repair the first time, especially since the battery and starter are already new.”
- Exit strategy: “Thank you. I’d like a written estimate tied to the test results, and if the data isn’t available today I’m going to pause authorization until the wet-condition testing is completed.”
- Never say: “My AI report says...” or “I got a second opinion online.”
- Always say: “I’ve done some research and want to understand...”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- For the primary repair, fair parts pricing for a crankshaft position sensor on a 2009 Civic is typically $60-$140 aftermarket or about $110-$190 OEM Honda/Denso-equivalent, depending on engine and supplier. A connector pigtail, if corrosion is present, usually adds $35-$90.
- Labor for CKP sensor access and harness repair is commonly 1.0-2.0 hours on the R18 engine, with another 0.5-1.0 hour if the splash shield, loom repair, or connector repinning is needed. At $120-$180 per labor hour, labor typically lands at $120-$540.
- Total fair installed price for the primary-cause repair is usually $220-$730 including diagnosis, depending on whether the shop only replaces the sensor or also repairs the connector and weather sealing.
- If the shop proposes an alternator first at $500-$1,000 without documented charging readings of 13.5-14.8 V running and cranking-voltage evidence below 9.6 V, that is not a data-driven repair for this symptom set.
- If they recommend all four coils, plugs, and an alternator together for a rain-related no-start without scope data or spark-test results, that is classic parts-cannon pricing rather than diagnosis.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts-cannon indicators on this Civic include immediate recommendations for alternator, starter, ignition switch, and fuel pump all at once despite a new battery and starter and no measured CKP/spark/power-feed data.
- Diagnostic shortcuts to watch for include a handheld battery/alternator tester used as the only basis for diagnosis, no live RPM check during crank, and no water simulation despite the complaint being rain-related.
- Price gouging red flags include charging 3.0+ labor hours for a simple CKP replacement with no harness work, billing four ignition coils before showing carbon tracking, or selling a fuse box assembly without voltage-drop proof at the affected terminals.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: one hour of focused diagnosis that includes live RPM during crank, CKP waveform capture, spark testing, and wet-condition simulation. Those tests directly separate the top three causes.
- Reject outright: blind alternator replacement, blanket ignition tune-up sales, or “let’s start with a fuel pump” without a failed fuel-pressure or power-feed test.
- Get a second opinion if the shop cannot provide actual readings in rpm, volts, and waveform form, or if they refuse to reproduce the rain condition with controlled water testing.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- Your Civic’s PCM needs three basics to start the R18 engine: crankshaft position input, ignition spark, and fuel delivery through the PGM-FI system. The starter motor only spins the engine; it does not prove the PCM knows where the crankshaft is.
- The CKP sensor sits in a harsh environment near the crank pulley and road splash. It generates a timing signal the PCM converts into engine speed, typically about 150-250 rpm during cranking. If that signal disappears, the PCM often withholds injector pulse and coil timing because it cannot synchronize combustion safely.
- Rain matters because water lowers insulation resistance and can bridge corroded terminals. A connector that measures fine dry can fail wet when a few hundred ohms of leakage distort a low-voltage sensor signal.
- Ignition coils fail differently. Each coil steps battery voltage into tens of thousands of volts. If a boot is cracked or carbon-tracked, spark can leak down the outside of the plug tube instead of jumping the plug gap, especially when moisture is present.
- Fuse-box or relay faults are power-distribution problems. Corroded terminals heat, build resistance, and may pass enough current for accessories but not enough for stable PCM or fuel-pump operation during crank.
- Prevention on a 2009 Civic is practical: keep the lower splash shield installed, inspect cowl drains, replace cracked coil boots, and reseal or repin any green-corroded connector before it becomes a stranded-in-rain failure.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- For a CKP repair, OEM Honda or a true OE supplier such as Denso/Hitachi is preferred because sensor amplitude and signal shape matter more than on simple switches. Cheap aftermarket CKP sensors can create intermittent sync issues even when “new.”
- Honda part numbers vary by VIN and engine calibration, so the shop should confirm by VIN before ordering. Ask them to print the Honda EPC line item for the crankshaft position sensor and, if needed, the repair-terminal or pigtail part number.
- For ignition coils, OEM Honda/Hitachi/Denso quality matters if the secondary cause is confirmed. Ultra-budget coils often create new misfire complaints within months.
- Pricing sources worth comparing are a Honda dealer parts counter, HondaPartsNow, and RockAuto for OE-brand equivalents. A fair strategy is OEM sensor or connector for the primary repair, with aftermarket only if it is a known OE manufacturer and the warranty is clear.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Anchor the conversation with the diagnostic path, not the symptom. Say, “If the live RPM is 0 during crank and the CKP waveform drops out wet, I’m comfortable approving the sensor or connector repair in the $220-$730 range.”
- If they quote above that range, ask what portion is diagnosis, what portion is harness repair, and how many labor hours are assigned. A justified quote should break out 1.0-2.0 hours mechanical access plus any connector repinning time.
- If they push an alternator, ask for charging voltage at idle and 2,000 rpm, loaded and unloaded, plus cranking voltage. Without readings like 13.5-14.8 V running and above 9.6 V cranking, the alternator sale lacks support.
- Walk away if they cannot produce scan data, scope captures, or voltage-drop numbers. Your leverage is that intermittent rain-related no-starts are solvable only with evidence, and shops that guess often end up eating comeback labor.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: crankshaft position sensor circuit moisture intrusion or connector corrosion, 46% confidence. The rain trigger, normal running once started, and lack of strong charging-system evidence fit a wet-sensitive CKP signal dropout best.
- Secondary cause: ignition coil boot or plug-well moisture causing weak/no spark during crank, 31% confidence. This is common on aging Hondas and weather-sensitive, but it is ranked below CKP because no misfire behavior or P0300-series code history was provided.
- Tertiary cause: under-hood fuse/relay box or PGM-FI main relay power-feed intermittency from corrosion/moisture, 23% confidence. This can absolutely cause a no-start in rain, but it usually leaves stronger clues such as fuel-pump prime loss, relay clicking anomalies, or broader electrical symptoms.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate action: schedule a diagnostic appointment only with a shop that has an oscilloscope and Honda-capable scan tool, and insist the vehicle be kept overnight or water-tested so the rain condition can be reproduced.
- Ask the shop to inspect the lower splash shield, CKP harness routing near the crank pulley, coil boots, plug wells, cowl drains, and under-hood fuse-box cover seal. Those are the highest-yield visual checks on a 2009 Civic with this complaint.
- If the primary cause is confirmed, replace the CKP sensor only if the waveform or connector condition proves it; otherwise repair the connector/pigtail and weather seal first. On older Hondas, the connector is often the real failure point.
- Future maintenance tied to this failure mode includes annual inspection of coil boots and plug wells, cowl drain cleaning before rainy season, and immediate repair of missing splash shields or broken harness retainers.
- Warning signs to monitor include extended crank time, tachometer staying dead during crank, no fuel-pump prime, rough running immediately after a wet start, or any new MIL with P0335/P0336 or P0300-P0304.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Honda service information for 2006-2011 Civic engine management and CKP/ignition diagnostics: https://techinfo.honda.com/rjanisis/logon.aspx
- NHTSA manufacturer communications and complaints database for 2009 Honda Civic electrical/engine issues, useful for checking related Honda bulletins and field patterns: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle/2009/HONDA/CIVIC
- iATN technical discussions and case studies on Honda intermittent rain-related no-start, CKP signal loss, and PGM-FI relay/fuse-box corrosion patterns: https://www.iatn.net/
- Ask the shop to verify any applicable Honda service bulletin affecting water intrusion, cowl sealing, or electrical connector corrosion by VIN in Honda iN/ServiceExpress, because bulletin applicability can change by production date and engine configuration.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Authorize only evidence-based diagnosis: live RPM during crank, CKP waveform capture, spark test, and wet-condition simulation.
- Do not approve an alternator, fuel pump, or full ignition parts package unless the shop shows the exact failed reading in volts, rpm, or waveform form.
- If the first shop cannot reproduce the rain-related no-start or provide printouts/photos, move the Civic to a Honda-experienced electrical diagnostician with a lab scope.
